title: The Right Measure for Physics-Constrained Generation:A Co-Area Correction for Posterior-Consistent PDE Inverse Problems

paper.title: The Right Measure for Physics-Constrained Generation: A Co-Area Correction for Posterior-Consistent PDE Inverse Problems
paper.abstract: Abstract Generative models—diffusion and flow matching—are increasingly used to solve partial differential equation (PDE) inverse problems, enforcing the governing physics as a hard constraint (via projection or guidance) and reporting the resulting samples as a Bayesian posterior with calibrated uncertainty. We show that this widely adopted recipe samples the wrong distribution. Conditioning a generative prior on a hard PDE constraint is conditioning on a measure-zero manifold—an operation that is intrinsically ambiguous (the Borel–Kolmogorov paradox) and whose physically correct resolution, the small-residual-noise limit, carries a co-area (Fixman) Jacobian factor [ det ( J J ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 [\det(JJ^{\!\top})]^{-1/2} that projection- and guidance-based methods silently omit. We make the bias precise, show that it grows with the heterogeneity of the constraint sensitivity, and validate it on controlled problems against an i.i.d. ground-truth arbiter. The omitted factor is not a second-order detail: removing it inflates the posterior error to 20 × 20\times the sampling-noise floor; minimal-displacement projection (as in PCFM) is biased at 9 × 9\times the floor; and a naive scalar reweighting does not fix it. We introduce CoCoS , a measure-aware constrained sampler that targets the correct co-area posterior, and show that it matches the gold-standard posterior to within sampling noise. Our results imply that “satisfying the physics” is not the same as “sampling the posterior,” and give a principled correction for uncertainty-aware scientific inference.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Deep generative models have become a powerful tool for scientific inference. For systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), conditional diffusion and flow-matching models are now used to reconstruct fields and infer parameters from sparse, noisy observations, with the appealing promise of fast, amortized, uncertainty-aware posterior sampling ( Yang et al. 2021 ; Bastek et al. 2025 ; Zang and Koutsourelakis 2025 ) . A central design question in this literature is how to make generated samples respect the governing physics. The dominant answers enforce the PDE (and conservation laws, boundary conditions, or data-consistency relations) as a hard constraint : either by projecting intermediate or final samples onto the constraint set ( Utkarsh et al. 2026 ; Li et al. 2026 ) , or by guiding the sampling dynamics with the constraint residual ( Parikh et al. 2026 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) . Having enforced the constraint, these methods report the resulting samples as draws from the Bayesian posterior and use them for uncertainty quantification (UQ). This paper questions the second step. Does enforcing the physical constraint actually produce samples from the posterior? We argue, and demonstrate, that for an important class of methods the answer is no—not by a small amount, and not because of an implementation detail, but because of a measure-theoretic subtlety inherited by any method that enforces the constraint post hoc and reports the result as a calibrated posterior. The issue is the following. A hard PDE constraint 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝟎 \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})=\bm{0} defines a lower-dimensional manifold ℳ = { 𝐱 : 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝟎 } \mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})=\bm{0}\} in the state space, which has measure zero under any continuous prior. Conditioning a distribution on such an event is the classical Borel–Kolmogorov ambiguity ( Trésor and Lukashchuk 2025 ) : the answer depends on how the zero-measure limit is taken. The physically meaningful choice is dictated by the modeling assumption that the PDE holds only up to small residual noise—numerical discretization, model error, finite-precision physics—i.e. 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , γ 2 ​ 𝐈 ) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\gamma^{2}\mathbf{I}) with γ → 0 \gamma\to 0 . By the co-area formula, this limit yields a conditional density on ℳ \mathcal{M} that is not the restriction of the prior, but the prior tilted by a Jacobian factor, p ⋆ ( 𝐱 ) ∝ π ( 𝐱 ) ℓ ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝐱 ) [ det ( J ( 𝐱 ) J ( 𝐱 ) ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 , 𝐱 ∈ ℳ , p^{\star}(\mathbf{x})\;\propto\;\pi(\mathbf{x})\,\ell(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})\,\big[\det\!\big(J(\mathbf{x})J(\mathbf{x})^{\!\top}\big)\big]^{-1/2},\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{M}, (1) where J = ∇ 𝐜 J=\nabla\mathbf{c} is the constraint Jacobian. Projection- and guidance-based methods target a different zero-measure limit (the Euclidean / perpendicular tube), and therefore omit the factor [ det ( J J ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 [\det(JJ^{\!\top})]^{-1/2} . The two limits coincide only when det ( J ​ J ⊤ ) \det(JJ^{\!\top}) is constant on ℳ \mathcal{M} —i.e. when the constraint sensitivity is spatially homogeneous, which it essentially never is for a PDE. The factor in ( 1 ) is well known in constrained molecular dynamics as the Fixman correction ( Fixman 1974 ) and underlies exact sampling of densities on implicitly-defined manifolds ( Lelievre et al. 2012 ; Zappa et al. 2018 ) ; our contribution is to show that it is exactly what is missing from physics-constrained generative inference, to quantify the resulting bias, and to give a corrected sampler.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • We identify and formalize a systematic bias in physics-constrained generative posteriors: enforcing a hard PDE constraint without the co-area/Fixman correction samples the wrong distribution, by a factor that scales with the heterogeneity of the constraint sensitivity (Thm. 1 , Cor. 1 , Prop. 2 ). • Using an i.i.d. rejection arbiter that is immune to the mixing pathologies that confound MCMC at small γ \gamma , we show on controlled problems that (i) the Fixman factor is necessary —omitting it gives 20 × 20\times the noise floor; (ii) minimal-displacement projection is biased ( 9 × 9\times ); and (iii) naive scalar reweighting is not a reliable fix. • We introduce CoCoS , a measure-aware constrained sampler that provably targets p ⋆ p^{\star} , and show it matches the gold-standard posterior to within sampling noise. • We discuss when the bias is largest and is therefore most consequential for scientific UQ, and the implications for the recent wave of physics-constrained generative models.

sections.heading: Scope (what we do and do not claim).
sections.text: The critique is specific, and we are careful not to overstate it. It targets methods that enforce the hard constraint post hoc on a fixed (pre)trained prior—minimal-displacement projection ( Utkarsh et al. 2026 ) or residual guidance ( Parikh et al. 2026 ; Kim et al. 2025 ) —and then report the constrained samples as a Bayesian posterior or use them for UQ ; for these, targeting the Euclidean rather than the residual limit makes the reported uncertainty miscalibrated (Sec. Experiments ). It does not indict (i) methods that seek only constraint- satisfying generation without a calibration claim, nor (ii) amortized inference trained on forward-simulated ( 𝜽 , 𝐲 ) (\bm{\theta},\mathbf{y}) pairs ( Sherki et al. 2025 ; Zhai et al. 2025 ) , which is measure-correct by construction (Prop. 4 )—a distinction we make precise and then exploit in CoCo-Flow. Soft-penalty training ( Bastek et al. 2025 ) targets a finite -noise posterior; it is biased only insofar as that noise is finite, and we include it as the γ > 0 \gamma{>}0 reference point. The contribution is thus to delineate when the bias occurs, quantify it, and correct it—not to claim every physics-constrained generator is wrong. Figure 1: The measure problem, and CoCoS fixes it. (a) Conditioning a prior (gray cloud) on the hard-constraint manifold ℳ \mathcal{M} yields a posterior whose uncertainty (red band) varies along ℳ \mathcal{M} : tight where the constraint is sensitive (steep) and broad where it is flat—the co-area weighting [ det ( J J ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 [\det(JJ^{\!\top})]^{-1/2} . (b) Resulting density on ℳ \mathcal{M} in a controlled 2 2 D example (constraint y = f ⁡ ( x ) y{=}f(x) ): CoCoS (green) recovers the true posterior (i.i.d. arbiter, shaded), whereas minimal-displacement projection (PCFM, blue dashed) systematically misplaces posterior mass—piling it where the manifold is flat and depleting the sensitive regions.

sections.heading: Physics-constrained generative models.
sections.text: A growing body of work injects PDE structure into diffusion/flow models. Soft-penalty approaches add a residual loss ( Bastek et al. 2025 ) and treat the physics–distribution tension as a multi-objective trade-off ( Baldan et al. 2026 ) . Hard-constraint approaches enforce 𝐜 = 𝟎 \mathbf{c}=\bm{0} exactly: PCFM ( Utkarsh et al. 2026 ) applies a minimal-displacement Gauss–Newton projection onto the tangent space of the constraint manifold at each sampling step, and gauge/convex-set methods ( Li et al. 2026 ) project onto structured feasible sets. All of these characterize “distributional fidelity” heuristically (e.g. optimal-transport alignment) and, as we show, none account for the co-area measure that conditioning on the constraint induces.

sections.heading: Posterior sampling for inverse problems.
sections.text: Training-free guidance methods steer a pretrained generative prior with the observation/PDE residual ( Parikh et al. 2026 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) , including source-space variants ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , and acknowledge that aggressive guidance “biases the sampling path.” A complementary line amortizes inference by forward simulation : conditional flow matching on joint ( 𝜽 , 𝐲 ) (\bm{\theta},\mathbf{y}) pairs ( Sherki et al. 2025 ; Zhai et al. 2025 ) and generative neural operators that learn the joint and invert it ( Zang and Koutsourelakis 2025 ) . As we show (Prop. 4 ), this forward-simulation route is automatically measure-correct—it never conditions on the manifold—which sharply distinguishes it from the projection/guidance methods that post-process a fixed prior and incur the co-area bias; we make this target explicit and use it to correct the latter. Bayesian PINNs ( Yang et al. 2021 ) provide an MCMC gold standard but are slow.

sections.heading: Sampling on manifolds.
sections.text: Exact sampling of a prescribed density on an implicitly-defined manifold is well studied in computational statistics and molecular dynamics: the Fixman potential ( Fixman 1974 ) , constrained Langevin dynamics ( Lelievre et al. 2012 ) , and Metropolis schemes with reverse-projection checks ( Zappa et al. 2018 ) . We import these tools into physics-constrained generative inference, where they have been absent.

sections.heading: Induced geometry (a natural-gradient analogy).
sections.text: The residual-noise model measures discrepancy in 𝐜 \mathbf{c} -space, not 𝐱 \mathbf{x} -space: to leading order it endows parameter space with the pullback metric J ⊤ ​ J J^{\!\top}J rather than the Euclidean 𝐈 \mathbf{I} , and the co-area factor [ det ( J J ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 [\det(JJ^{\!\top})]^{-1/2} is exactly the volume element of this induced metric on ℳ \mathcal{M} . Just as the natural gradient replaces the arbitrary Euclidean parameter metric with the Fisher–Rao metric, the co-area correction replaces the arbitrary ambient-Euclidean conditioning (projection) with the residual-induced one; the projection bias is the price of conditioning in the wrong metric.

sections.text: We target p ⋆ p^{\star} directly with an exact constrained sampler that is agnostic to the base geometry. sections.heading: Amortizing the correction (CoCo-Flow).
sections.text: The constrained sampler is exact but pays an MCMC cost per query. Because the correction lives entirely in the target measure , it can be moved to training time and amortized. We first note a clarifying fact: if a differentiable simulator is available, drawing joint pairs ( 𝜽 i , 𝐲 i ) (\bm{\theta}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i}) with 𝜽 i ∼ π \bm{\theta}_{i}\sim\pi , 𝐲 i = ℋ ⁡ ( 𝒢 ⁡ ( 𝜽 i ) ) + 𝜼 \mathbf{y}_{i}=\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{G}(\bm{\theta}_{i}))+\bm{\eta} and fitting a conditional flow q ϕ ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{\phi}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) by flow matching yields, as the noise level γ → 0 \gamma\to 0 , exactly the co-area posterior p ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐲 ) p^{\star}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{y}) —the joint draws respect the residual-tube measure by construction. The bias studied here arises specifically because projection/guidance/soft-penalty methods do not simulate the joint; they post-process a fixed (often pretrained) prior, which is where the measure is distorted. In that practically important regime—a fixed prior π \pi and a test-time constraint—we amortize by distilling the exact sampler: run Alg. 1 offline to produce teacher samples { 𝜽 i ∼ p ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐲 j ) } \{\bm{\theta}_{i}\sim p^{\star}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{y}_{j})\} over a distribution of constraints 𝐲 j \mathbf{y}_{j} , and train q ϕ ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{\phi}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) by conditional flow matching to reproduce them. Test-time inference is a single ODE solve—no Jacobian, no log det \log\det , no MCMC—so the co-area cost is paid once and amortized across unlimited queries. Equivalently, when the projection pushforward Jacobian is tractable one may skip MCMC and train directly against p ⋆ p^{\star} by co-area-reweighted flow matching, attaching to each projected anchor Π ⁡ ( 𝐱 0 ( i ) ) \Pi(\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(i)}) a self-normalized weight w i ∝ d ​ p ⋆ / d ⁡ ( Π # ​ π ) w_{i}\propto\mathrm{d}p^{\star}/\mathrm{d}(\Pi_{\#}\pi) whose dominant factor is the Fixman term [ det ( J J ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 [\det(JJ^{\!\top})]^{-1/2} . Either route produces a fast amortized generator that targets the measure-correct posterior, whereas existing amortized constrained generators inherit the bias of their (projected or soft-penalized) training data. sections.heading: Experiments
sections.text: Our goal is to test the central claim cleanly: is the co-area/Fixman correction the right target, and do existing physics-constrained samplers deviate from it? We isolate this from confounds (sampler mixing, the γ → 0 \gamma\to 0 gap) using an i.i.d. ground-truth arbiter.

sections.heading: Arbiter.
sections.text: The unambiguous definition of “prior conditioned on 𝐜 ≈ 𝟎 \mathbf{c}\approx\bm{0} ” is residual-band rejection: draw 𝐱 ∼ π \mathbf{x}\sim\pi and keep those with ‖ 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ‖ < ε \left\lVert\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert<\varepsilon . This is i.i.d. , free of mixing pathologies, and converges to p ⋆ p^{\star} as ε → 0 \varepsilon\to 0 . We verify band-convergence ( ε = 0.02 \varepsilon{=}0.02 vs. 0.01 0.01 ) and report a tight noise floor from two independent halves.

sections.heading: Controlled benchmark.
sections.text: We use a d = 4 d{=}4 problem with a single nonlinear (quadratic) constraint whose sensitivity ‖ ∇ 𝐜 ‖ \left\lVert\nabla\mathbf{c}\right\rVert varies 4.2 × 4.2\times over the posterior, a standard normal prior, and exact analytic gradients (no PDE-solver or autodiff confounds). We compare, against the rejection arbiter: the exact constrained sampler with the Fixman term (CoCoS), the same sampler without it (Hausdorff measure ∝ π \propto\pi ), minimal-displacement projection (PCFM), and PCFM with a scalar [ det J J ⊤ ] − 1 / 2 [\det JJ^{\!\top}]^{-1/2} reweighting. sections.heading: Findings (Table 1 ).
sections.text: (i) The Fixman factor is the correct target. CoCoS matches the arbiter to within the sampling-noise floor ( 0.010 0.010 vs. 0.004 0.004 ), confirming that the γ → 0 \gamma\to 0 hard-constraint posterior is the co-area density ( 1 ) and that the constrained sampler realizes it. (ii) It is necessary. Dropping the Fixman term (sampling the Hausdorff measure) is off by 21 × 21\times the floor. (iii) Projection is biased. PCFM deviates at 9 × 9\times the floor. (iv) Scalar fixes are unreliable. Post-hoc reweighting of projected samples does not recover the target—here it makes matters worse—because the projection pushforward is a curvature-dependent distortion, not a pure ‖ ∇ 𝐜 ‖ \left\lVert\nabla\mathbf{c}\right\rVert rescaling. An exact measure-aware sampler is required. We additionally found that an MCMC “gold standard” (HMC on the soft posterior at small γ \gamma ) is unreliable as an arbiter: it fails to mix in the stiff small- γ \gamma regime, masquerading as agreement under loose tolerances and as disagreement under tight ones. Only the i.i.d. arbiter resolves the question—a methodological point for the broader literature on evaluating physics-constrained posteriors.

sections.text: The ordering CoCoS ≪ \ll no-Fixman ≪ \ll PCFM is invariant across all three d = 8 d{=}8 instances and all three d = 16 d{=}16 instances. sections.heading: All three SOTA paradigms are biased, and the bias is a UQ error (Table 3 ).
sections.text: On a representative d = 8 d{=}8 instance we compare, against the same arbiter, methods from each paradigm: projection (PCFM), inference-time guidance (a guided Langevin sampler of the soft posterior, the mechanism shared by D-Flow / DiffusionPDE ( Parikh et al. 2026 ) ), and a soft-penalty / finite-noise posterior ( γ = 0.02 \gamma{=}0.02 , the target of PBFM/PIDM-style training ( Bastek et al. 2025 ; Baldan et al. 2026 ) ). All deviate from the true posterior (up to ∼ 40 × {\sim}40\times the floor), and crucially the deviation is a calibration failure, not a cosmetic one: averaged over the three instances, PCFM’s posterior standard deviation is wrong by 𝟗𝟔 % \mathbf{96\%} (and guidance by 56 % 56\% ), with miscalibrated 90 % 90\% intervals (coverage 0.95 0.95 / 0.93 0.93 ), while CoCoS matches the posterior spread to ∼ 1 % {\sim}1\% and is calibrated at 0.89 0.89 . For uncertainty-aware inference this is the difference between trustworthy and misleading error bars (Fig. 3 ). The full posterior covariance tells the same story (Fig. 2 ): CoCoS reproduces Σ \Sigma to 5 % 5\% (Frobenius), no-Fixman to 10 % 10\% , while PCFM is off by 𝟏𝟐𝟐 % \mathbf{122\%} —it invents correlations the posterior does not have. Across paradigms (projection, guidance, soft penalty), enforcing the constraint without the co-area term inflates both the distance to the posterior and the error in the reported uncertainty.

sections.heading: The bias is structured by sensitivity (Fig. 6 ).
sections.text: Figure 6 makes the mechanism explicit: binning samples by the constraint sensitivity det ( J ​ J ⊤ ) \sqrt{\det(JJ^{\!\top})} , the empirical density ratio of the no-Fixman (Hausdorff) sampler to the true posterior follows the predicted ∝ det ( J ​ J ⊤ ) \propto\sqrt{\det(JJ^{\!\top})} law almost exactly, and PCFM exhibits the same sensitivity-structured over-/under-representation. The bias is not noise—it is the missing co-area Jacobian, recovered quantitatively. The same conclusion is visible at the level of posterior marginals (Fig. 4 ): CoCoS overlays the arbiter, while projection is over-dispersed and shifted. Figure 4: Posterior marginals ( d = 8 d{=}8 Darcy). Three representative coordinates. CoCoS (green) matches the i.i.d. arbiter (shaded); minimal-displacement projection (PCFM, dashed) misplaces mass—over-dispersed tails and a depleted mode—i.e. a miscalibrated posterior, not a cosmetic shift.

sections.heading: Amortization: distilling CoCoS into a fast flow (CoCo-Flow).
sections.text: We test the amortized realization of Sec. CoCoS: Measure-Aware Constrained Sampling on a controlled d = 4 d{=}4 family with a scalar nonlinear observation y y (heterogeneous sensitivity). We generate measure-correct teacher samples (Prop. 4 ) and train a conditional flow-matching student q ϕ ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ y ) q_{\phi}(\bm{\theta}\mid y) ; test-time inference is a single ODE solve. At held-out y y , CoCo-Flow matches the rejection arbiter to 1.2 1.2 – 3.6 × 3.6\times the noise floor (mean ≈ 2.3 × {\approx}2.3\times ), whereas a student trained identically on projected samples inherits the projection bias ( 3.2 3.2 – 15 × 15\times the floor). The co-area correction survives amortization—and the measure of the training data is exactly what determines whether the fast generator is calibrated. The same recipe runs on the real d = 8 d{=}8 Darcy PDE: a conditional student q ϕ ​ ( 𝜽 ∣ 𝐲 ) q_{\phi}(\bm{\theta}\mid\mathbf{y}) trained once on forward-simulated pairs generalizes across held-out observations 𝐲 \mathbf{y} , matching the per- 𝐲 \mathbf{y} rejection arbiter at 5.7 × 5.7\times the floor on average (5 held-out 𝐲 \mathbf{y} ), with one-time training ( ∼ \sim 90 s) and ∼ \sim 56 ms per query—orders of magnitude faster than the minutes-per-query arbiter. This is looser than the exact sampler (the compact student is a coarse fit at d = 8 d{=}8 and is a target for better architectures), but it demonstrates that the correction amortizes on a real PDE and transfers across the observation. The same holds on a higher-dimensional nonlinear PDE: on d = 16 d{=}16 steady viscous Burgers, CoCo-Flow generalizes across 5 5 held-out 𝐲 \mathbf{y} at 5.0 × 5.0\times the floor ( 4.1 4.1 – 5.8 × 5.8\times ), with ∼ \sim 96 s one-time training and 29 29 ms per query—confirming the amortized route runs and generalizes beyond the linear, low-dimensional setting.

sections.heading: A nonlinear PDE, and when the bias is small.
sections.text: On a 1 1 D steady viscous Burgers inverse problem with mild sensitivity heterogeneity, the three samplers are nearly indistinguishable ( 1.8 1.8 / 2.2 2.2 / 2.3 × 2.3\times the floor for CoCoS/no-Fixman/PCFM)—consistent with Corollary 1 : where det ( J ​ J ⊤ ) \det(JJ^{\!\top}) varies little, projection is approximately unbiased. The bias is a function of sensitivity heterogeneity, exactly as the theory predicts; it is largest on the strongly heterogeneous Darcy problems and negligible here. The quantity that governs the bias—the constraint sensitivity det ( J ​ J ⊤ ) \sqrt{\det(JJ^{\!\top})} —is here vastly more heterogeneous than in 1D: it spans more than five orders of magnitude, varying by 2.6 × 𝟏𝟎 𝟓 × \mathbf{2.6{\times}10^{5}\times} across the posterior (vs. 12 12 – 33 × 33\times at d = 8 / 16 d{=}8/16 ). By Corollary 1 this is exactly the regime in which the co-area correction matters most. Measured over all d = 64 d{=}64 coordinates the projection bias appears small ( 3 × 3\times the floor), but this is an artifact: with m = 3 m{=}3 observations, ∼ 61 {\sim}61 directions are prior-dominated (unidentified) and dilute the per-coordinate average. Restricting to the likelihood-informed subspace ( Cui et al. 2014 ) —the top- 6 6 eigenvectors of the posterior-averaged J ⊤ ​ J J^{\!\top}J , i.e. the directions the data actually constrains—PCFM is biased at 21.7 × \mathbf{21.7\times} the floor, squarely matching the 1D Darcy magnitudes and confirming the bias scales to the field-valued regime. sections.heading: When does the bias bite?
sections.text: The deviation between projection/guidance and the true posterior scales with the spatial variation of the constraint sensitivity det ( J ​ J ⊤ ) \det(JJ^{\!\top}) and with the misalignment between the base model’s off-manifold geometry and the residual directions. When sensitivity is homogeneous the bias vanishes; for PDEs—where sensitivity is dictated by the operator and the observation pattern—it is generically present and largest exactly where it matters most for UQ (poorly-constrained, high-sensitivity directions).

sections.heading: Rank deficiency and weak identifiability.
sections.text: Assumption 1 (full-rank J J on ℳ \mathcal{M} ) is generic but, in sparse-observation PDE inverse problems, G = J ​ J ⊤ \mathrm{G}=JJ^{\!\top} is often near -singular along weakly-identified directions, so [ det G ] − 1 / 2 [\det\mathrm{G}]^{-1/2} can be large. Three points. (i) This is the correct Bayesian behaviour, not a pathology : a direction the data barely constrains should be prior-dominated, and the co-area weight up-weights it by exactly the amount the residual tube widens there; the singularity is integrable when rank drops on a set of co-area–measure zero, and the finite-noise soft posterior p γ p_{\gamma} ( γ > 0 \gamma{>}0 , Eq. 6 ) is a proper density regardless of rank—which is what CoCoS and the rejection arbiter actually sample. (ii) CoCoS’s regularization does not bias the target. The constrained step solves with ( G + ϵ ​ 𝐈 ) − 1 (\mathrm{G}+\epsilon\mathbf{I})^{-1} , but the Metropolis acceptance uses the exact potential ( 5 ) and a reverse-projection check, so ϵ \epsilon affects only the proposal , never the invariant law p ⋆ p^{\star} (Thm. 2 ); we additionally winsorize the rare near-singular log det G \log\det\mathrm{G} terms. This is a structural advantage over projection/guidance, where any such regularization directly biases the reported samples. (iii) If one instead regularizes the target (Tikhonov: G → G + ϵ ​ 𝐈 \mathrm{G}\!\to\!\mathrm{G}+\epsilon\mathbf{I} inside ( 5 )), one samples a controlled relaxation p ϵ ⋆ p^{\star}_{\epsilon} with p ϵ ⋆ ⇒ p ⋆ p^{\star}_{\epsilon}\Rightarrow p^{\star} as ϵ → 0 \epsilon\to 0 —a quantifiable approximation, not a hidden one. Empirically our 2D Darcy is squarely in this regime— det G \sqrt{\det\mathrm{G}} spans more than five orders of magnitude (median ∼ 10 − 13 {\sim}10^{-13} , range up to ∼ 2.6 × 10 5 {\sim}2.6{\times}10^{5} )—and the FD-verified Jacobian and the i.i.d. arbiter both remain stable.

sections.heading: Cost and scaling.
sections.text: The correction requires the constraint Jacobian J J (already formed by projection-based methods) and an m × m m\times m log-determinant; for large codimension the latter can be estimated stochastically (Hutchinson). The amortized realization CoCo-Flow moves this cost to training time so that test-time inference is a single ODE solve; a full empirical study of the amortized generator—including conditioning across observation operators and scaling to field-valued 𝜽 \bm{\theta} —is the natural next step.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Enforcing a PDE constraint is not the same as sampling the posterior. Hard-constraint generative methods condition on a measure-zero manifold and, by targeting the wrong zero-measure limit, omit a co-area/Fixman Jacobian that is necessary for correctness. We made the bias precise, validated it against an i.i.d. arbiter, and gave a measure-aware sampler that recovers the true posterior. For uncertainty-aware scientific inference, getting the measure right is not optional.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2606.04804v1 [cs.LG] 03 Jun 2026 The Right Measure for Physics-Constrained Generation: A Co-Area Correction for Posterior-Consistent PDE Inverse Problems Jian Xu Delu Zeng John Paisley Qibin Zhao Abstract Generative models—diffusion and flow matching—are increasingly used to solve partial differential equation (PDE) inverse problems, enforcing the governing physics as a hard constraint (via projection or guidance) and reporting the resulting samples as a Bayesian posterior with calibrated uncertainty. We show that this widely adopted recipe samples the wrong distribution. Conditioning a generative prior on a hard PDE constraint is conditioning on a measure-zero manifold—an operation that is intrinsically ambiguous (the Borel–Kolmogorov paradox) and whose physically correct resolution, the small-residual-noise limit, carries a co-area (Fixman) Jacobian factor [ det ( J J ⊤ ) ] − 1 / 2 [\det(JJ^{\!\top})]^{-1/2} that projection- and guidance-based methods silently omit. We make the bias precise, show that it grows with the heterogeneity of the constraint sensitivity, and validate it on controlled problems against an i.i.d. ground-truth arbiter. The omitted factor is not a second-order detail: removing it inflates the posterior error to 20 × 20\times the sampling-noise floor; minimal-displacement projection (as in PCFM) is biased at 9 × 9\times the floor; and a naive scalar reweighting does not fix it. We introduce CoCoS , a measure-aware constrained sampler that targets the correct co-area posterior, and show that it matches the gold-standard posterior to within sampling noise. Our results imply that “satisfying the physics” is not the same as “sampling the posterior,” and give a principled correction for uncertainty-aware scientific inference. 1 RIKEN iTHEMS 2 RIKEN AIP 3 South China University of Technology 4 Columbia University jian.xu@riken.jp Introduction Deep generative models have become a powerful tool for scientific inference. For systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), conditional diffusion and flow-matching models are now used to reconstruct fields and infer parameters from sparse, noisy observations, with the appealing promise of fast, amortized, uncertainty-aware posterior sampling ( Yang et al. 2021 ; Bastek et al. 2025 ; Zang and Koutsourelakis 2025 ) . A central design question in this literature is how to make generated samples respect the governing physics. The dominant answers enforce the PDE (and conservation laws, boundary conditions, or data-consistency relations) as a hard constraint : either by projecting intermediate or final samples onto the constraint set ( Utkarsh et al. 2026 ; Li et al. 2026 ) , or by guiding the sampling dynamics with the constraint residual ( Parikh et al. 2026 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) . Having enforced the constraint, these methods report the resulting samples as draws from the Bayesian posterior and use them for uncertainty quantification (UQ). This paper questions the second step. Does enforcing the physical constraint actually produce samples from the posterior? We argue, and demonstrate, that for an important class of methods the answer is no—not by a small amount, and not because of an implementation detail, but because of a measure-theoretic subtlety inherited by any method that enforces the constraint post hoc and reports the result as a calibrated posterior. The issue is the following. A hard PDE constraint 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝟎 \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})=\bm{0} defines a lower-dimensional manifold ℳ = { 𝐱 : 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = 𝟎 } \mathcal{M}=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})=\bm{0}\} in the state space, which has measure zero under any continuous prior. Conditioning a distribution on such an event is the classical Borel–Kolmogorov ambiguity ( Trésor and Lukashchuk 2025 ) : the answer depends on how the zero-measure limit is taken. The physically meaningful choice is dictated by the modeling assumption that the PDE holds only up to small residual noise—numerical discretization, model error, finite-precision physics—i.e. 𝐜 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , γ 2 ​ 𝐈 ) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\gamma^{2}\mathbf{I}) with γ → 0 \gamma\to 0 . Contributions. • We identify and formalize a systematic bias in physics-constrained generative posteriors: enforcing a hard PDE constraint without the co-area/Fixman correction samples the wrong distribution, by a factor that scales with the heterogeneity of the constraint sensitivity (Thm. 1 , Cor. 1 , Prop. 2 ). • Using an i.i.d. rejection arbiter that is immune to the mixing pathologies that confound MCMC at small γ \gamma , we show on controlled problems that (i) the Fixman factor is necessary —omitting it gives 20 × 20\times the noise floor; (ii) minimal-displacement projection is biased ( 9 × 9\times ); and (iii) naive scalar reweighting is not a reliable fix. • We introduce CoCoS , a measure-aware constrained sampler that provably targets p ⋆ p^{\star} , and show it matches the gold-standard posterior to within sampling noise. • We discuss when the bias is largest and is therefore most consequential for scientific UQ, and the implications for the recent wave of physics-constrained generative models. Related Work Physics-constrained generative models. A growing body of work injects PDE structure into diffusion/flow models. Soft-penalty approaches add a residual loss ( Bastek et al. 2025 ) and treat the physics–distribution tension as a multi-objective trade-off ( Baldan et al. 2026 ) . Hard-constraint approaches enforce 𝐜 = 𝟎 \mathbf{c}=\bm{0} exactly: PCFM ( Utkarsh et al. 2026 ) applies a minimal-displacement Gauss–Newton projection onto the tangent space of the constraint manifold at each sampling step, and gauge/convex-set methods ( Li et al. 2026 ) project onto structured feasible sets. All of these characterize “distributional fidelity” heuristically (e.g. optimal-transport alignment) and, as we show, none account for the co-area measure that conditioning on the constraint induces. Posterior sampling for inverse problems. Training-free guidance methods steer a pretrained generative prior with the observation/PDE residual ( Parikh et al. 2026 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Jiang et al. 2025 ) , including source-space variants ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , and acknowledge that aggressive guidance “biases the sampling path.” A complementary line amortizes inference by forward simulation : conditional flow matching on joint ( 𝜽 , 𝐲 ) (\bm{\theta},\mathbf{y}) pairs ( Sherki et al. 2025 ; Zhai et al. 2025 ) and generative neural operators that learn the joint and invert it ( Zang and Koutsourelakis 2025 ) . As we show (Prop. 4 ), this forward-simulation route is automatically measure-correct—it never conditions on the manifold—which sharply distinguishes it from the projection/guidance methods that post-process a fixed prior and incur the co-area bias; we make this target explicit and use it to correct the latter. Bayesian PINNs ( Yang et al. 2021 ) provide an MCMC gold standard but are slow. Sampling on manifolds.
